items.title: commands.catalog returns /compact as both command and alias, causing 'Duplicate slash command alias' error in Desktop/SDK clients

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

items.body:
## Problem

The `commands.catalog` RPC (in `tui_gateway/server.py`) returns `/compact` in **two conflicting ways** within the same response:

### 1. As a command → from `_TUI_EXTRA`
```python
_TUI_EXTRA = [
    ("/compact", "Toggle compact display mode", "TUI"),  # line 11172
    ...
]
```
This adds `"/compact"` to `pairs[]`, so clients register `/compact` as a **command**.

### 2. As an alias → from `COMMAND_REGISTRY` canon map
```python
# hermes_cli/commands.py line 92
CommandDef("compress", ..., aliases=("compact",)),
```
The `canon` dict in `commands.catalog` includes `{"/compact": "/compress"}`, so clients register `compact` as an **alias** of `/compress`.

### The conflict
When a client (Hermes Desktop, SDK, or any consumer of `commands.catalog`) processes the response:
1. It registers `compact` as a **command** (from `pairs`)
2. It then tries to register `compact → compress` as an **alias** (from `canon`)
3. Since `compact` already exists as a command, it throws: **"Duplicate slash command alias: /compact"**

In the Hermes Desktop app (https://github.com/fathah/hermes-desktop), this error surfaces as a full-screen modal that makes the app unusable.

## Root Cause
`/compact` in `_TUI_EXTRA` serves a TUI-specific purpose (toggle compact display mode), but `compact` was also registered as an alias of `/compress` in the main command registry. The catalog builder has no dedup logic to catch that a `_TUI_EXTRA` entry collides with a canon alias.

## Proposed Fix

**Option A** (minimal, backward-compatible): Rename the TUI extra entry to avoid the alias collision:
```python
# tui_gateway/server.py line 11172
("/compact-display", "Toggle compact display mode", "TUI"),
```

**Option B** (more thorough): In the `commands.catalog` handler, skip alias entries from `canon` when the alias name also appears as a standalone entry in `pairs` or `_TUI_EXTRA`.

## Files Affected
- `tui_gateway/server.py` — `_TUI_EXTRA` list (line 11172)
- `hermes_cli/commands.py` — `compress` command with `compact` alias (line 92)

## Environment
- Hermes v0.17.0
- Hermes Desktop v0.7.1

items.title: Async delegation result delivered to wrong TUI session after context compression

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Bug Description

When multiple TUI sessions coexist in the desktop GUI, a background async delegation (`delegate_task(background=true)`) result can be delivered to the **wrong session** — not the session that dispatched it.

## Root Cause

The `completion_queue` is process-wide (shared across all TUI sessions). Each session's notification poller (`_notification_poller_loop` in `tui_gateway/server.py`) drains this queue and uses `_notification_event_belongs_elsewhere()` to filter events.

The filter compares `evt["session_key"]` against `session["session_key"]`. However, **context compression changes `session_key`** — compression creates a new continuation session with a new ID, and `session["session_key"]` is updated to the new ID (see comment at `server.py:565-567`):

```python
# Use session_id (from agent.session_id) not session_key — after compression,
# session_key may be stale (the ended parent) while session_id is the live
# continuation. Fix for #20001.
```

When session A dispatches a background delegation, the event records session A's `session_key` at dispatch time. If session A then undergoes context compression, its `session_key` changes. The event still carries the **old** `session_key`.

If a **different** session B's compression chain happens to have passed through the same session ID (because compression creates a parent→child chain of session IDs), session B's poller will see the event's `session_key` as matching its own (stale or historical) `session_key`, and consume the event.

## Evidence (from agent.log)

```
2026-07-03 14:51:39 [20260703_143836_b93d00] Dispatched async delegation batch deleg_549935bc (1 task(s), session_key=20260703_142228_a27e8b)
2026-07-03 14:55:04 [20260702_173700_f85b0c] conversation turn: session=20260702_173700_f85b0c msg='[ASYNC DELEGATION BATCH COMPLETE — deleg_549935bc]'
```

- Delegation dispatched from session `20260703_143836_b93d00` with `session_key=20260703_142228_a27e8b`
- Result delivered to session `20260702_173700_f85b0c` (a completely different session)
- The `session_key=20260703_142228_a27e8b` matched because session `20260702_173700_f85b0c`'s compression chain had previously passed through `20260703_142228_a27e8b`

## Affected Code

1. **`tui_gateway/server.py:8210-8237`** — `_notification_event_belongs_elsewhere()`: only compares current `session_key`, doesn't account for compression history
2. **`tui_gateway/server.py:8286-8308`** — Poller comment already acknowledges the risk: *"If multiple TUI sessions coexist, whichever poller wakes first grabs the event"*
3. **`tools/async_delegation.py:312-314`** — Event records `session_key` at dispatch time, which becomes stale after compression
4. **`tui_gateway/server.py:565-567`** — Compression changes `session_key` (documented but not handled in delegation routing)

## Suggested Fix

Two options:

### Option A: Track compression chain (robust)

Store the full compression chain (list of session IDs from original to current) in each session dict. `_notification_event_belongs_elsewhere()` should check if `evt["session_key"]` is in the current session's compression chain, not just equal to the current `session_key`.

### Option B: Use a stable session identifier (simpler)

Add a `stable_session_id` that persists across compression (set at session creation, never changed). Record this in delegation events and compare against it in the filter.

## Environment

- Platform: Windows 10, Hermes desktop GUI (TUI mode)
- Multiple active TUI sessions in the same process
- Context compression enabled (default threshold 0.50)
- `delegation.max_async_children: 3`

## Impact

- Background delegation results are silently delivered to the wrong conversation
- The receiving session's agent may act on results it didn't request (in our case, an audit report from another session was processed and acted upon)
- The dispatching session never receives its result — it appears lost

items.title: Electron renderer process leak causes OOM killer cascade (~2700 child processes)

labels.name: sweeper:cannot-reproduce
labels.description: Sweeper: could not reproduce on current main

items.body:
## Bug Description

Hermes Desktop (Electron app) leaks renderer/GPU child processes when the rendering subsystem crashes. The parent process keeps spawning new `io.flutter.ui` children without cleaning up the old ones, leading to an explosion of thousands of processes that exhaust all available RAM and trigger the kernel OOM killer.

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-35-generic
- GPU: NVIDIA (driver loaded)
- Hermes Desktop: Electron-based
- RAM: 32GB + 8GB swap
- Desktop scaling: `--force-device-scale-factor=2`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Leave Hermes Desktop running overnight (idle state)
2. Renderer/GPU process crashes at some point (possibly related to NVIDIA driver or high DPI scaling)
3. Electron keeps spawning replacement `io.flutter.ui` processes
4. Old crashed processes are never reaped
5. After several hours, ~2700 child processes accumulate
6. System runs out of memory → OOM killer cascade

## Observed Behavior

OOM killer struck at 05:29 AM on 2026-07-03, killing 7 processes sequentially:

```
05:29:06  Hermes Desktop (PID 19856, RSS 189MB, oom_score_adj: 300)
05:31:24  Feishu (PID 17641, RSS 136MB, oom_score_adj: 300)
05:33:21  Chrome (PID 18382, RSS 44MB, oom_score_adj: 300)
05:36:14  Chromium (PID 2874792, RSS 30MB, oom_score_adj: 300)
05:39:48  llama-server (PID 468665, RSS 594MB, oom_score_adj: 200)
05:43:04  hermes-gateway (PID 2400397, RSS 38MB, oom_score_adj: 200)
05:45:01  warp-taskbar (PID 140422, RSS 212MB, oom_score_adj: 200)
```

Kernel log shows ~2,700 `io.flutter.ui` processes were active at the time of OOM, each with ~1.1GB virtual memory and ~32MB RSS. The total memory consumed by these leaked processes was approximately 86GB.

## Expected Behavior

Crashed renderer processes should be reaped and not infinitely respawned. There should be a cap on the number of child processes spawned by the Electron app.

## Logs

```
Jul 03 05:20:01 systemd-journald: Under memory pressure, flushing caches
Jul 03 05:29:06 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 19856 (Hermes) total-vm:1460064884kB, anon-rss:189048kB
Jul 03 05:29:05 systemd: app-gnome-hermes\x2ddesktop-19796.scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'
[... 6 more OOM kills follow ...]
```

## Impact

All user applications killed while user was asleep. Lost state in Chrome, Feishu, WeChat, and other running apps.

## Suggested Fix

1. Add a max-child-process limit for Electron renderer processes
2. Implement proper cleanup of crashed renderer processes before spawning replacements
3. Consider a health-check mechanism that kills the parent if the child count exceeds a threshold (e.g., 50)

items.title: [Bug]: Plugin-registered web providers can't be selected via web.extract_backend

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

items.body:
### Bug Description

Setting `web.extract_backend` to the name of a provider that was registered by a **plugin** (as opposed to one of the built-in backends) is silently ignored. `web_extract()` ends up dispatching to a different, auto-detected backend instead of surfacing an error or honoring the configured plugin.

**Impact:** Any web-extract or web-search plugin that introduces a new provider name (not in the hardcoded list in `_is_backend_available()`/`_get_backend()`) cannot be selected via `web.extract_backend` / `web.search_backend` / `web.backend` — the config is silently overridden by whatever backend auto-detection happens to pick, with no error or warning to the user.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install a web-extract plugin that registers a provider under a custom name, e.g. a local plugin at `.hermes/plugins/web/pageprune/` with `plugin.yaml` declaring:
   ```yaml
   provides_web_providers:
     - pageprune
   ```
2. Set the following in `.hermes/config.yaml`:
   ```yaml
   web:
     backend: ''
     search_backend: exa
     extract_backend: pageprune
   ```
3. Make sure another backend's credentials are also present in the environment (e.g. `TAVILY_API_KEY`).
4. Start Hermes and ask the agent to fetch/extract the content of a URL (triggers `web_extract`).
5. Check `.hermes/logs/agent.log`.

### Expected Behavior

`web_extract()` should dispatch the URL extraction through the `pageprune` provider, as explicitly configured in `web.extract_backend`.

### Actual Behavior

Plugin discovery correctly finds and registers the plugin:
```
INFO hermes_cli.plugins: Plugin 'web-pageprune' registered web provider: pageprune
INFO hermes_cli.plugins: Plugin discovery complete: 55 found, 31 enabled
```

But `web_extract` dispatches to `tavily` instead of `pageprune`:
```
INFO tools.web_tools: Web extract via tavily: 1 URL(s)
INFO plugins.web.tavily.provider: Tavily extract: 1 URL(s)
```

`TAVILY_API_KEY` happens to be set in the environment, which is why `tavily` is chosen — with no key set, a similarly wrong (but different) backend would be picked instead. Either way, the explicit `extract_backend: pageprune` setting is never honored, and no warning or error is surfaced to the user.

### Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`tools/web_tools.py` still resolves the extract backend through a **legacy** helper chain that predates the plugin-based provider registry, and that chain uses a hardcoded backend allow-list that doesn't include plugin-provided names:

- `web_extract()` calls `backend = _get_extract_backend()` at [tools/web_tools.py:709](hermes-agent/tools/web_tools.py#L709)
- `_get_extract_backend()` → `_get_capability_backend("extract")` → checks `_is_backend_available(specific)` at [tools/web_tools.py:199-209](hermes-agent/tools/web_tools.py#L199-L209)
- `_is_backend_available()` only recognizes a fixed set of names — `exa`, `parallel`, `firecrawl`, `tavily`, `searxng`, `brave-free`, `ddgs`, `xai` — and returns `False` for anything else, including `pageprune` ([tools/web_tools.py:212-238](hermes-agent/tools/web_tools.py#L212-L238))
- Because `"pageprune"` fails that check, `_get_capability_backend` discards it and falls through to `_get_backend()` ([tools/web_tools.py:139-171](hermes-agent/tools/web_tools.py#L139-L171)), which reads `web.backend` (empty here) and then auto-detects from env vars, landing on `tavily` because `TAVILY_API_KEY` is set.
- Back in `web_extract()` ([tools/web_tools.py:724](hermes-agent/tools/web_tools.py#L724)), `provider = _wsp_get_provider(backend)` now looks up `"tavily"` (not `"pageprune"`) in the registry, finds it, and uses it directly — the correct, plugin-aware fallback `get_active_extract_provider()` ([agent/web_search_registry.py:232](hermes-agent/agent/web_search_registry.py#L232)) is only reached if the registry lookup for `backend` fails, which doesn't happen here since `tavily` *is* a valid, registered provider.

Notably, `agent/web_search_registry.py` already implements the correct resolution logic and is plugin-aware: `get_active_extract_provider()` / `_resolve()` ([agent/web_search_registry.py:133-219](hermes-agent/agent/web_search_registry.py#L133-L219)) explicitly documents "explicit config wins, ignoring availability" and works against the live `_providers` registry rather than a hardcoded list. The bug is that `web_extract()`/`web_search()` consult the old `_get_extract_backend()`/`_get_search_backend()` first and only fall back to the correct resolver as an afterthought.

The same bug affects `web_search()` via `_get_search_backend()` at [tools/web_tools.py:571](hermes-agent/tools/web_tools.py#L571) for any plugin-registered search provider not in the hardcoded allow-list.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

In `web_search()` and `web_extract()`, resolve the active provider directly via the registry (`get_active_search_provider()` / `get_active_extract_provider()`) instead of first computing a backend name through `_get_search_backend()` / `_get_extract_backend()` and looking it up by name. The registry resolver already implements the desired precedence (explicit per-capability config → shared `web.backend` → single eligible provider → legacy preference order) and is aware of plugin-registered providers, so this removes the need to keep a hardcoded backend allow-list in sync with every provider plugin that can be installed.

items.body:
### Bug Description

After new `Custom endpoint` is configured as the default `model`, resuming a previous session no longer works.

For example, previous sessions of mine used OpenRouter with Opus. The new custom endpoint I switched to is Featherless with GLM. Every time I try to resume an old session, it fails with:

```
error: resume failed: Model anthropic/claude-opus-4.8 has a context window of 2,048 tokens, which is below the minimum 64,000 required by Hermes Agent.  Choose a model with at least 64K context, or set model.context_length in config.yaml to override.
```

The context window numbers are wrong. This is because Hermes tried to resume the session using the last known Opus config, but hitting up the new Featherless endpoint, which is wrong.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Set up Hermes with Opus via OpenRouter by using `Hermes model`
2. Start `Hermes` and start a session with a prompt, maybe chat a few turns.
3. Exit
4. Use `hermes model` to change to a `Custom endpoint`
   - paste `https://api.featherless.ai/v1` for the endpoint
   - Paste your API key
   - choose the OpenAI chat completions URL format
   - Edit `config.yaml` to add `max_tokens: 32768` to the `model` section or it won't work due to https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/51773
5. Start `hermes`
6. Use `/sessions` to resume the previous session
7. Observe the error

### Expected Behavior

It should resume.

### Actual Behavior

Instead it tries to connect to Featherless using details of the previous OpenRouter/Opus configuration, which causes the error.

### Workaround

Set `model.context_length` to a high enough number in config.yaml (`256000` in my case for Featherless). This bypasses the context check for all models.

Note that the session will continue with the previous `model` provider, not with the newly selected main model. Note that `model.context_length` may artificially limit your context size based on the new model (OpenRouter Opus accepts 1M, but in my case it is set to 256k so that Featherless will work). Use `/model` to change the model.

Configuration (config.yaml, .env, hermes setup)

# Root Cause Hint (by Hermes using GLM via Featherless)

The error is caused by a bug in `_BARE_BILLING_PROVIDERS` in `tui_gateway/server.py:1482`:


_BARE_BILLING_PROVIDERS = {"auto", "openrouter", "custom"}


When you resume an old Opus session, here's the chain of events:

1. Session row: model=anthropic/claude-opus-4.8, billing_provider=openrouter, model_config=NULL
2. `_stored_session_runtime_overrides` (line 1485): reads billing_provider="openrouter". Since "openrouter" is in _BARE_BILLING_PROVIDERS, it drops the provider override —leaves it as None. ### Summary

The stdio MCP client gives up **permanently** after 5 failed reconnect attempts (`tools/mcp_tool.py`, `_MAX_RECONNECT_RETRIES = 5` — line 289 on current `main`, give-up path around line 2442). Once it gives up, the MCP server stays dead for the life of the gateway process: every subsequent tool call returns `{"error": "MCP server '<name>' is not connected"}` instantly (0.00s — no reconnect is attempted on use). Only a full gateway restart recovers it.

Additionally, the retry counter is never reset after a *successful* reconnect, so on long-uptime gateways transient blips accumulate toward guaranteed permanent death even if each individual blip recovers.

### Real-world failure

- hermes-agent **0.16.0**, Ubuntu 24.04 VM, stdio MCP server wrapped over SSH.
- A ~30-minute network outage (router-side) hit the box on 2026-07-02.
- Log sequence: `keepalive failed, triggering reconnect` → `connection lost (attempt 1/5 … 5/5)` → `failed after 5 reconnection attempts, giving up` (10:15:44–10:18:18 local).
- Hours later, with the network long recovered and the underlying SSH transport verified healthy, a tool call still returned `MCP server 'openbrain' is not connected` instantly.
- **Contrast:** the Telegram platform loop in the same gateway rode out the *same* outage (≈10 retries with backoff) and self-healed. The MCP client is the only component that died permanently.

### Suggestion

1. After the retry budget is exhausted, attempt a **lazy reconnect on next tool call** instead of failing instantly (or use unbounded backoff like the platform loops).
2. **Reset the retry counter after a successful reconnect** so the cap applies per-outage, not per-process-lifetime.

Happy to provide fuller logs if useful.

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Bug Description

When multiple Hermes gateways run simultaneously with different `--profile` flags, the cron scheduler resolves `script` paths against whichever profile happens to execute the tick — not the profile that owns the job. This causes script-not-found errors that rotate through different profiles on each run.

## Root Cause

1. Cron jobs are stored globally at `~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json`, not profile-scoped
2. Each gateway's scheduler reads the same `jobs.json` and competes to execute jobs
3. The `script` field is a relative path resolved against `~/.hermes/profiles/<current_profile>/scripts/` at execution time — where `<current_profile>` is whichever scheduler wins the tick

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create multiple profiles: `hermes profile create alice`, `hermes profile create bob`
2. Place a script at `~/.hermes/scripts/test.sh`
3. Create a cron job with `script: "test.sh"` under profile `alice`
4. Run two gateways: `hermes --profile alice gateway run` and `hermes --profile bob gateway run`
5. Wait for the cron tick — it alternates between looking in `alice/scripts/` and `bob/scripts/`

## Expected Behavior

- Either the script path should be resolved at creation time and stored as an absolute path
- Or the cron scheduler should only execute jobs that belong to its own profile
- Or `jobs.json` should be profile-scoped (under `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/cron/`)

## Actual Behavior

Cron output rotates through different profiles each run:

```shell
# Day 1
Script not found: ~/.hermes/profiles/wjc/scripts/hermes-backup.sh
# Day 2
Script not found: ~/.hermes/profiles/yls/scripts/hermes-backup.sh
# Day 3
Script not found: ~/.hermes/profiles/cfm/scripts/hermes-backup.sh
```

## Environment

- OS: macOS 15.4
- Hermes version: latest (multiple profile gateways running simultaneously)
- Cron job config: `no_agent: true`, `script: "hermes-backup.sh"`

## Workaround

Copy the script to every profile's `scripts/` directory. Not ideal for maintenance.

## Suggested Fix

Option A: Store the resolved absolute path in the job at creation time.
Option B: Scope `jobs.json` per-profile like sessions/skills/memory already are.
Option C: Add an ownership field to each job so schedulers skip jobs that don't belong to their profile.

items.title: /compress shows misleading "No changes from compression" when lock is held

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## The lie

`/compress` says "No changes from compression" when compression never ran. Another process (dashboard, another TUI, gateway, auto-compress) holds the session lock — the command silently returns messages unchanged.

Three callsites, same lie:

| Where | What you see | What actually happened |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| CLI `/compress` | "No changes from compression" | Dashboard held the lock, compress never ran |
| Gateway `/compress` | "No changes from compression" | Same |
| TUI `session.compress` | "No changes from compression" | Same |

The worst case: a session with 200+ messages and ~200k tokens says `(._.) Not enough conversation to compress (need at least 4 messages)`.

## Root cause

`_compress_context` in `agent/conversation_compression.py` (line 555) returns `(messages, existing_sp)` — unchanged — when lock acquisition fails. No signal to callers. Lock-held, aux-model failure, and genuine no-op all look identical. Callers pass unchanged messages through `summarize_manual_compression`, which sees identical before/after and reports `noop=True`.

## Fix

`_compress_context` sets `agent._compression_skipped_due_to_lock` when lock acquisition fails. Each caller checks this signal before reporting results. Signal is cleared at entry to prevent stale leakage (auto-compress skip → later manual false positive).

See PR #57634.

items.body:
Describe the bug：

QQ Bot adapter fails to connect because connect() method signature doesn’t match the base class. The base class BasePlatformAdapter.connect() expects an is_reconnect keyword argument, but QQAdapter.connect() doesn’t accept it.

Steps to Reproduce：

1. Configure QQ Bot in config.yaml (AppID / AppSecret)
2. Start gateway: hermes gateway run
3. See error: QQAdapter.connect() got an unexpected keyword argument 'is_reconnect'
4. QQ Bot stays offline (“soul is not online.”)

Expected Behavior:

QQ Bot should connect successfully and respond to messages.

Actual Behavior:

Gateway fails to connect QQ Bot and keeps retrying with the same error.

Logs:

    ERROR gateway.run: ✗ qqbot error: QQAdapter.connect() got an unexpected keyword argument 'is_reconnect'

Environment:

- Hermes Agent version: v0.18.0
- File: gateway/platforms/qqbot/adapter.py:281

Root Cause:

- base.py defines: async def connect(self, *, is_reconnect: bool = False) -> bool:

- adapter.py has: async def connect(self) -> bool:

The is_reconnect parameter was added to the base class but QQ Bot adapter was not updated.

Workaround:

Change line 281 in gateway/platforms/qqbot/adapter.py from:

    async def connect(self) -> bool:

to:

    async def connect(self, *, is_reconnect: bool = False) -> bool:

### Problem or Use Case

Hermes already has broader requests around conversation export (for example #57233 and #51200), but there is a narrower workflow that would be useful on its own: exporting only the prompts the user typed in a single session, with their original order and timestamps.

This is useful for prompt review, reproducing a workflow, task retrospectives, and sharing a clean prompt timeline without assistant responses, tool calls, tool outputs, system messages, or internal traces.

### Proposed Solution

Add a prompt-only export mode for a single session. The export should include:

- session id
- 1-based prompt index within the session
- prompt creation timestamp, preferably ISO-8601 with timezone if available
- raw user prompt text
- optional message id/event id if available in the session store

Possible CLI shapes:

```sh
hermes sessions export-prompts <session_id> --format jsonl
hermes sessions export <session_id> --only user-prompts --format markdown
```

JSONL example:

```jsonl
{"index":1,"created_at":"2026-07-03T10:15:20Z","role":"user","text":"..."}
{"index":2,"created_at":"2026-07-03T10:18:42Z","role":"user","text":"..."}
```

Markdown example:

```md
# User prompts for session abc123

## 1. 2026-07-03T10:15:20Z
...

## 2. 2026-07-03T10:18:42Z
...
```

### Privacy / Scope

The point of this mode is to be intentionally minimal. It should not export assistant messages, tool calls, command output, system prompts, hidden context, memory payloads, or compaction summaries.

### Acceptance Criteria

- Exports only user-authored prompts from the selected session.
- Preserves stable chronological/session order.
- Includes prompt timestamps when available.
- Supports at least one machine-readable format such as JSONL.
- Does not change the existing full-session export behavior.

### Feature Type

CLI / session export

### Scope

Prompt timeline export for one session.

items.title: [Bug]: holographic memory auto_extract harvests context-compaction summaries into fact_store, and runs even when configured off

labels.name: area/memory
labels.description: Memory subsystem: store, providers, sync, background reviews

items.body:
## Bug Description

Two compounding defects in `plugins/memory/holographic/__init__.py` cause context-compaction handoff summaries to be persisted as durable "facts" in `memory_store.db`. They then re-surface in holographic recall and pollute future sessions with stale meta-text.

**Defect 1: string-boolean gate.** The `on_session_end` gate is:

```python
if not self._config.get("auto_extract", False):
    return
```

The plugin's own config schema declares `auto_extract` as a string enum: `{"key": "auto_extract", ..., "default": "false", "choices": ["true", "false"]}`. A config carrying the quoted string `'false'` (as materialized from the schema default; observed in our install) is truthy, so `not 'false'` is `False` and extraction runs despite being configured off. #53575 (merged) fixed the adjacent case where byterover ignored `auto_extract` entirely; the open `is_truthy_value()` sweeps #56446 / #50050 / #51122 do not cover this plugin.

**Defect 2: no compaction-summary filter.** `_auto_extract_facts` regex-scans every `role == "user"` message. The compaction handoff summary can be inserted as a `role="user"` message (see the `summary_role` selection in `context_compressor.compress` and the `_find_last_user_message_idx` docstring). Summary prose reliably matches `_DECISION_PATTERNS` (`we decided/agreed/chose`, `the project uses/needs/requires`), so the compactor's own output is stored verbatim as a `project` fact, truncated to 400 chars.

Defect 2 stands alone: even with `auto_extract` intentionally enabled, compaction summaries get harvested as facts. Defect 1 is what made it fire for users who believe the feature is off.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Holographic memory provider active, config containing the string form `auto_extract: 'false'` (the plugin schema's default materializes as this string).
2. Run a session long enough to trigger context compaction.
3. End the session so `on_session_end` fires.
4. Inspect the store:
   ```bash
   sqlite3 ~/.hermes/memory_store.db \
     "SELECT fact_id, substr(content,1,80), category FROM facts ORDER BY fact_id DESC LIMIT 3"
   ```

## Expected Behavior

- `auto_extract: 'false'` (string) disables extraction, same as boolean `false`.
- Compaction/handoff summaries are never eligible for fact extraction, regardless of the `auto_extract` setting.

## Actual Behavior

A `project`-category fact beginning `[CONTEXT COMPACTION — REFERENCE ONLY] Earlier turns were compacted into the summary below...` appears after each rollover that follows a compaction. Deleting it does not help; the next rollover re-creates it from the next summary. Observed twice in consecutive rollovers:

```
2026-07-03 10:28:27,402 INFO [20260703_100256_d0494d] plugins.memory.holographic: Auto-extracted 1 facts from conversation
2026-07-03 10:35:32,995 INFO [20260703_102827_c09a58] plugins.memory.holographic: Auto-extracted 1 facts from conversation
```

Each log line correlates with a new compaction-summary fact row (`created_at` matches).

## Affected Component

Agent Core (memory / context compression): `plugins/memory/holographic/__init__.py`, interaction with `agent/context_compressor.py`.

## Suggested Fix

- Gate: coerce with the shared truthy helper, e.g. `if not is_truthy_value(self._config.get("auto_extract", False)): return`, and/or make the schema emit real booleans. Mirrors merged #53575 and the pattern in open #56446 / #50050.
- Eligibility: in `_auto_extract_facts`, skip synthetic summary messages before pattern matching. The infrastructure already exists in `agent/context_compressor.py`: summary messages carry `COMPRESSED_SUMMARY_METADATA_KEY` (`"_compressed_summary"`) metadata, and `_is_context_summary_content()` detects the sentinel prefix including the merged-into-tail case. Checking the metadata key with the content-prefix check as fallback (metadata may not survive all session-store round-trips) covers it.

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (VM)
- Python: 3.11.15 (venv)
- Hermes: v0.18.0 (2026.7.1), upstream b14d75f8
- Bug verified present on current `main` by inspecting the raw files today (gate, schema default, and `_auto_extract_facts` unchanged; file last touched by 7c0a5def)

Debug note: root cause is identified at source level with exact references above, so no debug bundle is attached; happy to run `hermes debug share` if you still want one.

## Related

- #22907 / #22959: `auto_extract` stores raw messages verbatim (extraction quality). Distinct issue: this one is about which messages are eligible. #22959's derivation patch would still harvest compaction summaries.
- #53575 (merged): byterover `auto_extract` config no-op.
- #56446, #50050, #51122 (open): `is_truthy_value()` coercion sweeps that do not touch this plugin.

items.title: Windows Desktop installer stalls at 0%: `install-main.ps1` is spawned directly and fails when `.ps1` association is Notepad

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Summary

Hermes Desktop on Windows can stall at the very first bootstrap step because it appears to spawn `install-main.ps1` directly instead of invoking it through PowerShell.

On Windows, `.ps1` files are commonly associated with Notepad / edit-preview behavior rather than direct execution. In that state, the Desktop installer logs a bootstrap failure and never reaches the Python/Node/Git dependency stages.

This makes the documented “one-click Desktop install” fail before the installer visibly starts doing useful work.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Account type: local Windows account, not Microsoft account
- Installer: Hermes Desktop / `Hermes-Setup.exe`
- Initial attempted custom home: `M:\AI\Hermes\home`
- Later attempted default Desktop install path: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes`
- `.ps1` association at time of failure: Notepad / non-executable association

## What happened

After launching `Hermes-Setup.exe`, the Desktop UI appeared stuck at the initial install/bootstrap screen. The progress did not advance into the expected dependency installation flow.

The `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` folder contained only:

```text
bootstrap-cache
logs
```

It did **not** proceed to create/install the expected Python/Node/Git/runtime folders.

The log showed:

```text
install script invocation failed e=spawning install-main.ps1
Caused by: program not found
```

## Expected behavior

Hermes Desktop should not depend on the user’s global `.ps1` file association.

It should invoke the bootstrap script explicitly through PowerShell, for example conceptually:

```powershell
powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <path-to>\install-main.ps1
```

or another explicit bundled runner.

## Actual behavior

The Desktop app appears to attempt to spawn `install-main.ps1` as if it were directly executable. On this Windows machine, that fails before dependency installation begins.

Result:

- UI appears stuck at 0% / initial bootstrap
- No Python/Node/Git dependency install begins
- Only `bootstrap-cache` and `logs` are created
- User is left with no actionable error in the GUI

## Why this matters

The Desktop installer is documented and promoted as the easy path for non-terminal users. This failure mode makes the “one-click install” experience break on a normal Windows configuration where `.ps1` files are not directly executable.

A non-technical user will interpret this as a failed or frozen installer, even though the log contains the root cause.

## Suggested fixes

1. Invoke `install-main.ps1` via `powershell.exe -File` or an explicit PowerShell runner instead of spawning the `.ps1` directly.
2. Surface the bootstrap error in the Desktop UI instead of leaving the progress screen stuck.
3. Add a preflight check for PowerShell availability and execution policy.
4. Document the fallback CLI install command in the Desktop UI when bootstrap fails.
5. Avoid recommending or relying on users changing global `.ps1` file associations, since that weakens Windows script-safety behavior.

## Related UX issue

During recovery attempts, the setup flow also routed the user into Nous Portal / subscription / credit-card onboarding, which was confusing for a user trying to use ChatGPT / OpenAI OAuth as the provider. It would help if the Desktop wizard more clearly separated:

- Nous Portal subscription setup
- OpenAI OAuth / ChatGPT provider setup
- API-key providers

This issue is mainly about the Windows Desktop bootstrap failure, but the provider-selection UX compounded the debugging confusion.

items.body:
# `security.redact_secrets: true` rewrites the text of *executed* commands, corrupting them (not just redacting logs)

## Summary

With `security.redact_secrets: true`, secret-shaped substrings are replaced with `***` inside the command/script text that is actually handed to the shell / interpreter — not only in transcripts and logs. Any command that legitimately carries a token (an `Authorization` header, an inline constant that pattern-matches a credential) executes corrupted and fails in ways that look like agent coding errors, so the agent burns turns "debugging" syntax instead of recognizing redaction.

## Environment

- hermes-agent v0.16.0 (Docker image `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v2026.6.5`), self-hosted gateway, Telegram platform, `terminal.backend: local`
- Also checked v2026.7.1 source: the redaction code paths involved appear unchanged, so we expect the behavior to persist (not re-reproduced live on 7.1 yet)
- `security.redact_secrets: true` (default)

## Observed failures (from 8 weeks of session transcripts, ≥14 distinct sessions)

1. **Executed Python rewritten.** The agent ran a `python3 << 'PYEOF'` heredoc containing a line assigning a project id to a variable whose name matched a secret pattern. The *interpreter's own error output* shows the mutated source:

   ```
   File "<stdin>", line 2
       API_KEY=*** = '307218'
                     ^^^
   SyntaxError: invalid syntax
   ```

   i.e. the heredoc text was rewritten to `API_KEY=***` **before** being fed to `python3`'s stdin — the `***` reached the interpreter.

2. **`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` header mangled in-flight.** curl calls to a PostgREST API with a JWT in the header failed with:

   ```
   JWSError (CompactDecodeError Invalid number of parts: Expected 3 parts; got 4)
   ```

   and `bad_jwt ... invalid number of segments` — consistent with the redactor splicing `***` into the middle of the JWT (turning 3 dot-separated segments into 4). Reproduced across 7 distinct sessions.

3. **bash sees the placeholder.** Gateway log line:

   ```
   /usr/bin/bash: line 8: Authorization: Bearer *** bad substitution
   ```

4. **Read-path blanking misleads env checks.** `echo GH=${#GH_TOKEN}` printed `GH=0` while the variable was set and non-empty (a sibling variable with a non-reserved name printed its real length in the same session). The agent then reported the credential as "missing" to the operator. (We understand `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN` are additionally reserved/stripped by the env blocklist — the confusing part is that redaction makes *any* secret look absent when echoed, and the two mechanisms are indistinguishable from inside a session.)

## Expected behavior

Redaction should apply to what is *displayed and persisted* (transcripts, logs, streaming output) — never to the string handed to the shell/interpreter/subprocess. The executed bytes must be exactly what the model wrote.

## Impact

- Every workflow that sends an auth header from `terminal` breaks nondeterministically.
- Failures masquerade as the model's syntax errors, so the agent retries variations instead of diagnosing redaction — expensive turn loops.
- Work-around we've adopted (100% reliable): never inline a secret in a command; `write_file` a script that reads `os.environ` and execute the file. Consider documenting this, but the write-path corruption still feels like a bug worth fixing at the source.

## Repro sketch

1. `security.redact_secrets: true`
2. Ask the agent to run: `curl -s https://httpbin.org/headers -H "Authorization: Bearer $SOME_TOKEN"` where `SOME_TOKEN` is any JWT-shaped env value, via the `terminal` tool.
3. Observe the request fail / the header arrive mutated, and the transcript show `***` inside the executed command.

### Problem or Use Case

The desktop and TUI status-bar context-window gauge only refreshes on `message.complete`. During a long agentic turn — often several minutes across dozens of tool calls — the gauge stays frozen at the previous turn's value, then jumps once at the end.

This matters because the context gauge is the operator's primary early-warning signal during exactly those long turns: *is this turn about to run into the context window / trigger compression?* Today you can't tell whether you're at 40% or 95% until the turn ends — by which point compression may already have fired or the turn failed on context. The frustrating part is that the data is already there: the agent updates its session token counters and the compressor's window-occupancy reading after **every internal API call** (`conversation_loop.py`); the gateway just never delivers them mid-turn.

For comparison, other agent frontends already treat this as table stakes: Claude Code's status line "runs after each new assistant message … debounced at 300ms" ([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline.md)), so its context figure visibly climbs during a multi-tool turn. A frozen gauge in Hermes desktop/TUI reads as "broken" next to that.

### Proposed Solution

Gateway-side live usage ticks, reusing existing machinery end to end:

- While `run_conversation` is in flight, a lightweight per-turn ticker samples the existing `_get_usage()` snapshot at 1 Hz and emits a `session.usage` event with the payload wrapped as `{"usage": ...}` — the same shape `message.complete` / `session.info` already use, so clients keep a single reading convention.
- Ticks whose snapshot is identical to the previous one are skipped, so the frame rate is bounded by *actual change* (per API call), not by the sampling rate; a single long API call produces zero redundant frames.
- Desktop and TUI merge the tick into the status-bar usage store, scoped to the focused session (a background turn must not move the active bar).

No change to core tool schemas, no coupling of the agent core to the gateway, and no impact on prompt caching. As a side hardening, the desktop's existing `message.complete` usage write gets the same focused-session guard, fixing a latent bug where a finishing background turn could overwrite the focused session's gauge.

Implementation (with backend + frontend tests) is open at #52119.

### Alternatives Considered

- **Push from the core loop where the counters increment** — lowest latency, but couples the agent core to the gateway (or requires observer plumbing through `run_conversation`), and a token-increment hook would miss non-token snapshot fields (`active_subagents`, `compressions`) that whole-snapshot sampling picks up for free. With change-detection, 1 Hz sampling is observationally equivalent to push + debounce (Claude Code debounces to 300 ms anyway).
- **Token-level streaming usage from inside an API call** — a much larger surface (per-provider stream normalization) and a different concern; per-API-call granularity is what the counters natively provide and matches what comparable tools ship.
- **Client-side polling via a new JSON-RPC request** — N clients × M sessions polling is heavier than one server-side ticker per *running* turn, and needs a new request type; the event push reuses the existing channel and matches the established `_start_notification_poller` pattern in the gateway.

### Feature Type

Gateway / messaging improvement

### Scope

Medium (few files, < 300 lines)

### Contribution

- [x] I'd like to implement this myself and submit a PR — implementation already open at #52119.

items.body:
## Summary

If `MEMORY.md` or `USER.md` on disk contains invalid UTF-8 bytes, memory is silently disabled for the entire agent session, with **zero log output**. There is no signal for an operator to diagnose why memory stopped working.

## Root cause

`MemoryStore._read_file()` in `tools/memory_tool.py` only catches `(OSError, IOError)` around the decode:

```python
# tools/memory_tool.py:691-694 (before fix)
try:
    raw = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
except (OSError, IOError):
    return []
```

`Path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on invalid UTF-8 bytes. `UnicodeDecodeError` is a subclass of `ValueError`, **not** `OSError`/`IOError`, so it is not caught here — it propagates up.

The caller, `agent_init.py`, wraps the entire memory bootstrap in a broad catch-all:

```python
# agent/agent_init.py:1239-1253
if not skip_memory:
    try:
        ...
        agent._memory_store = MemoryStore(...)
        agent._memory_store.load_from_disk()   # <-- raises UnicodeDecodeError here
    except Exception:
        pass  # Memory is optional -- don't break agent init
```

The `except Exception: pass` swallows the `UnicodeDecodeError` completely. Result: `agent._memory_store` stays `None`, `agent._memory_enabled`/`agent._user_profile_enabled` are left set from config (so the system *thinks* memory is on), and nothing is ever printed or logged. The failure is indistinguishable from "memory just isn't there this session" unless someone reads the source and reasons about exception hierarchies.

## Reproduction (PoC)

```python
from pathlib import Path
from tools.memory_tool import MemoryStore

p = Path("/tmp/MEMORY.md")
p.write_bytes(b"\xff\xfe invalid utf8 bytes")

result = MemoryStore._read_file(p)
# UnicodeDecodeError raised inside _read_file, uncaught by (OSError, IOError),
# propagates to agent_init.py's bare `except Exception: pass` in a real run.
```

Any bit-flip, partial write, disk corruption, wrong-encoding manual edit, or an external tool writing non-UTF-8 bytes into either memory file will trigger this — silently, every session, until someone manually inspects the file bytes.

## Impact

- Memory (both agent notes and user profile) silently stops working for the whole session.
- No log line, no warning, no error surfaced anywhere — operators have no starting point to debug from.
- Because `agent._memory_enabled` stays `True` from config, any code checking that flag believes memory is active when it is not.

## Suggested fix

Catch `UnicodeDecodeError` explicitly in `_read_file()` (it will not be caught by `except (OSError, IOError)`) and log a visible error before degrading to an empty entry list, so the corruption is diagnosable instead of silently swallowed.

## Fix

Implemented in PR (this branch): `fix/memory-encoding-corruption-silent-disable`.

items.title: Desktop always activates Default profile on startup — ignores is_active from API
items.body:
## Bug Description

Hermes Desktop always activates the Default (root) profile on startup, ignoring the `is_active` field from the API. Custom profiles set via `hermes profile use <name>` are never auto-activated.

**Reproduced on the latest version (v0.18.0).**

## Root Cause

The desktop app uses `is_default` (which identifies the structural root profile `~/.hermes`) instead of `is_active` (which reflects the user's sticky default from `hermes profile use <name>`) in all profile selection logic.

Affected files:

**`apps/desktop/src/app/profiles/index.tsx:81`** — initial profile selection on load:
```ts
return list.find(p => p.is_default)?.name ?? list[0]?.name ?? null
```

**`apps/desktop/src/store/profile.ts:357`** — `switchToDefaultProfile()`:
```ts
const def = $profiles.get().find(profile => profile.is_default)
```

**`apps/desktop/src/app/chat/sidebar/profile-switcher.tsx:143`** — sidebar default profile:
```ts
const defaultProfile = profiles.find(profile => profile.is_default)
```

**`apps/desktop/src/store/profile.ts:346,350,365`** — `orderedProfileKeys()` filters/hardcodes based on `is_default`.

All of these should key off `is_active` for the "which profile should be active on startup" decision.

## Context from hermes-webui

Previously reported as [nesquena/hermes-webui#4722](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/issues/4722). The maintainer clarified:

- `is_default` — identifies the structural root profile. Intentionally hardcoded. By design.
- `is_active` — indicates the currently-active / sticky default profile. Follows `active_profile` correctly.

The webui issue was closed with the conclusion that **clients should key off `is_active`** for startup profile selection.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a named profile: `hermes profile create shared`
2. Set it as sticky default: `hermes profile use shared`
3. Verify: `cat ~/.hermes/active_profile` → `shared`
4. Open Hermes Desktop
5. Observe: the Default (root) profile is active, not "shared"

## Expected Behavior

On startup, Hermes Desktop should check `is_active` from the profile list API and automatically activate whichever profile has `is_active: true`. If `shared` was set via `hermes profile use shared`, the desktop should start with `shared` active — not Default.

items.title: Desktop should skip auto-update when connected to a remote backend
items.body:
## Problem

When Hermes Desktop is connected to a **remote backend** (e.g., Desktop on Mac → Gateway in a Docker container), the Desktop app still checks for and applies updates automatically. This triggers a destructive cascade:

1. Desktop detects new commits → runs `hermes update` to pull and rebuild
2. Update process calls `_kill_stale_dashboard_processes()` which kills all dashboard processes
3. The desktop-managed backend (the one the Desktop is connected to remotely) gets caught in the kill
4. Gateway receives SIGTERM from s6-supervise → enters a boot→kill→reboot→restart loop
5. Desktop gets stuck on "Loading" for minutes, showing:
   - `Cached remote Hermes backend failed liveness probe; dropping stale connection.`
   - `Desktop boot failed: Your remote gateway session has expired.`

In the Desktop log this appears as:
```
[Hermes] [updates] update: Updating Hermes (git + dependencies)…
[Hermes] Hermes backend exited (SIGTERM)
[Hermes] [boot] Restarting desktop connection
[Hermes] [boot] Desktop boot failed: Your remote gateway session has expired.
```

And in the gateway log, the gateway dies and restarts multiple times within minutes (21:02 → 21:05 → 21:06 → 21:08 → 21:09 all SIGTERMed by s6-supervise).

## Root Cause

In remote-backend mode, the Desktop app is a **WebSocket client** — not a local Hermes instance manager. The `DESKTOP_BACKEND_CONTRACT` version check already handles compatibility warnings between Desktop and backend versions. The backend has its own lifecycle management (Docker/s6/systemd) and should NOT be touched by the Desktop auto-update.

## Proposed Fix

In the Desktop update flow (`applyUpdatesPosixInApp` or equivalent), check if the active connection is remote. If so:

1. **Skip the auto-update check entirely** — do not check for new commits, do not pull, do not rebuild
2. Only verify `DESKTOP_BACKEND_CONTRACT` compatibility
3. If the backend is stale, show a warning banner instead of triggering an update

This is not about adding a config option. This is about recognizing that **remote mode is a fundamentally different operating mode** where the Desktop has no business auto-updating.

## Related Issues

| Issue | Relevance |
|-------|-----------|
| [#37532](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/37532) | The kill-loop mechanism: `_kill_stale_dashboard_processes` kills desktop-managed backends |
| [#42354](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/42354) | Same symptom: Desktop fails to reconnect after update in remote mode (WSL user) |
| [#40018](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/40018) | Right direction but doesn't go far enough — proposes opt-in for remote backend update, but remote mode should not auto-update at all |
| [#29846](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/29846) | Side effect: users get annoying gateway shutdown notifications from auto-update restarts |

## Environment
- Desktop: macOS (Mac ARM64), connected to remote backend at `localhost:9119`
- Backend: Hermes Agent in Docker container (OrbStack), managed by s6 supervision
- Gateway: feishu + weixin platforms

labels.name: comp/agent

items.body:
## Description

When `ContextCompressor.compress()` finds no compressible window (`compress_start >= compress_end`), it returns the input messages unchanged. However, `compress_context()` does not detect this no-op and proceeds with full session rotation (`end_session` + `create_session`), writing back almost the same message list.

On the next turn, the preflight compression check sees tokens still above the threshold and re-triggers compression, creating an infinite loop where each pass saves only 2-3 tool output lines (474->472 messages, ~5% token reduction) and rotates to a fresh child session.

## Observed Impact

A session had 17 compression rotations in ~4 hours. Each child session contained only 0-4 messages before being compressed again. The original session had 699 messages; after each rotation the compressed transcript stayed at ~474 messages / ~207K tokens, far above the 128K threshold.

The anti-thrashing guard (`_ineffective_compression_count >= 2`) stops the loop within a single turn, but the next turn's preflight check re-triggers it because the compressed messages still exceed the threshold.

## Root Cause

`agent/conversation_compression.py` - `compress_context()` does not check whether the compressor made any progress before rotating the session.

## Suggested Fix

In `agent/conversation_compression.py`, after `compressed = agent.context_compressor.compress(...)`, check if `len(compressed) == len(messages)` and skip session rotation if so. The compressor already has anti-thrashing logic (`_ineffective_compression_count` in `should_compress()`), but it is defeated because `compress_context()` unconditionally rotates the session — writing back almost the same message list — even when the compressor made no progress. Each rotation perpetuates the problem by persisting the same context for the next turn's preflight check.

A local fix is available: see the Update comment below for the patch.

items.title: Windows: atomic_replace drops writes on ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION (concurrent reader of gateway_state.json et al.)

labels.name: comp/agent

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows, `atomic_replace()` in `utils.py` silently drops writes whenever any other process (or thread) holds an ordinary read handle on the target file. `os.replace` fails with `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` → `PermissionError` (EACCES), which is **not** in the helper's copy-fallback set (`EXDEV`/`EBUSY` only), so the exception propagates to callers — most of which swallow it — and the freshly-written `.tmp` file is orphaned next to the target.

## Why this happens

CPython opens files on Windows without `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`. Renaming *onto* a file that another handle has open is therefore denied, even though opening it for write would succeed. Any read/write collision on the same file turns the "atomic" write into a no-op:

- `gateway/run.py` `_persist_active_agents()` rewrites `gateway_state.json` at **every turn boundary**
- `gateway/status.py` `read_runtime_status()` (and the status dashboard pollers) read the same file concurrently

So on an active Windows gateway this is not a rare race — status updates are dropped routinely, and orphaned `.gateway_state_*.tmp` files accumulate in the profile directory. It affects **every** `atomic_json_write` / `atomic_yaml_write` caller (config writes, auth, cron state, …), not just gateway state.

## Reproduction (Windows)

```python
import json, utils
target = "gateway_state.json"
utils.atomic_json_write(target, {"active_agents": 1})
with open(target) as reader:              # any concurrent reader
    utils.atomic_json_write(target, {"active_agents": 2})
# → PermissionError: [WinError 32] before the fix; .tmp file left behind
```

## Proposed fix

In `atomic_replace()`, treat `PermissionError`/`EACCES` on Windows as a member of the fallback class:

1. **Bounded retry** of `os.replace` first (a few × ~20 ms) — sharing violations from transient readers usually clear within milliseconds, and the retry preserves atomicity.
2. If the handle is still held, **fall back to copy/fsync/unlink** (the existing EXDEV/EBUSY path) so the write lands instead of being dropped. The copy is not atomic, which is why the rename is retried first.

POSIX behavior is unchanged: there `EACCES` means directory permissions, the copy fallback would fail identically, and the error should keep propagating.

Found during an adversarial review of the proprioception plugin work, but the defect is platform-wide in the shared helper.

Environment: Windows 11, Python 3.11, hermes-agent @ `def6d6fe1`.

## 问题

Hermes 的 memory 有 2200 字符硬限制。当记忆超过阈值时，`memory_guard.py` 会将长条目迁移到 `fact_store`，在 memory 中替换为指针格式（如 `→ fact_store id#83`）。

但 fact_store 不会自动注入到会话上下文。用户必须主动调用 `fact_store(action="probe")` 才能看到迁移出去的内容。这导致：

1. **知识断层**：迁移出去的记忆在需要时不会被自动看到
2. **指针空洞**：memory 注入的指针只是提醒"有东西在那儿"，无法替代实际内容
3. **CLv2 差距**：相比 ECC CLv2 的 observer-loop 自动扫描+推送，Hermes 缺少"迁移后自动召回"的机制

## 场景

```
memory 注入 → 读到 "架构终态 v3 → fact_store id#83"
              ↓
            这是一条指针，但 id#83 的实际内容需要主动 probe
              ↓
            只有当 agent 恰好记得去查，且关键词匹配，才能看到
```

## 建议实现

在 session 初始化的 system prompt 构建阶段（`agent/prompt_builder.py`），扫描 memory 条目中的 `fact_store id#\d+` 引用模式，自动 resolve 对应条目内容，追加到上下文。

实现方式（二选一）：

**方案 A：内联展开**
```
[memory 条目原文]
架构终态 v3 → fact_store id#83  ← 注入时自动替换为实际内容
```

**方案 B：附录区块**
```
## 引用的持久事实（自动展开）
- id#83: 架构终态 v3(2026-07-03)：Hermes=大脑+唯一入口...
- id#79: 抖音视频下载正确流程...
```

两种方案都确保 agent 不需要"想起去查"就能看到完整内容。

## 参考资料

- 现有实现：`memory_guard.py` 的 auto_migrate 功能、`agent_memory.py` 的三层记忆
- 触发讨论的实际案例：2026-07-03 会话中，抖音视频下载流程从 memory 迁移到 fact_store 后，需要手动 probe 才能查看

items.body:
## Motivation

MoA (Mixture of Agents) is currently only available on the desktop app and CLI. Users who primarily interact with Hermes through messaging gateway platforms (WeChat, Feishu, Discord, Telegram, Slack, etc.) cannot benefit from multi-model parallel reasoning — each message is processed by a single model in the default pipeline.

## Use Case

A user sends a complex query (e.g., "analyze this stock and recent AI industry news") via WeChat/Feishu. With MoA on gateway:
- One reference model could analyze financial data (via Wind MCP)
- Another reference model could search current AI news (via web_search)
- The aggregator synthesizes both into a single reply

Without it, the user must manually switch models or rely on serially chained tool calls, losing the parallel reasoning advantage of MoA.

## Technical Considerations

1. **Latency**: Gateway platforms have different timeout expectations than desktop/CLI. MoA adds advisor round-trips. Solutions:
   - Allow configurable advisor timeout per gateway platform
   - Stream partial results progressively (already being worked on for desktop)
   - Only trigger MoA on explicit `/moa` command flag in message

2. **Streaming**: MoA streaming on gateway currently has bugs (#57251). Gateway streaming needs to be robust before this can work.

3. **Cost visibility**: Gateway users need to know MoA consumes multiple model calls. Show cost breakdown in reply footer (similar to desktop session cost tracking).

## Existing Related Issues
- #53698 Feishu: add shortcut UX for internal Hermes commands like /moa
- #53682 WebUI: support internal slash commands like /moa (fixed in v0.18.0)
- #57251 MoA streaming: APIConnectionError on gateway platforms (blocker)

## Suggested Approach
1. Add `moa.enabled_on_gateway` config toggle (default: false)
2. Support `/moa` slash command on gateway platforms (building on #53698, #53682 patterns)
3. Allow gateway-specific MoA presets (e.g., faster/cheaper advisor models for chat)
4. Fix streaming on gateway (#57251) as prerequisite

items.title: [Bug]: protect_first_n decay state is in-memory — a gateway restart re-protects old compaction summaries, head grows unboundedly

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: area/memory
labels.description: Memory subsystem: store, providers, sync, background reviews

items.body:
### Bug Description

After a gateway restart, the next compaction of an already-compacted session re-applies `protect_first_n` head protection. The previous `[CONTEXT COMPACTION]` summary (plus whatever stray messages sit next to it) gets copied verbatim into the protected head, and the new summary is stacked after it. Every restart+compaction cycle adds another layer — the head grows unboundedly, which is exactly the failure mode the protect-decay (#11996) was built to prevent.

Post-compaction message list of a long-lived production session (sanitized request dump, 2026-07-02):

```
[0] system    (persona)
[1] user      <arbitrary mid-session message, verbatim>  ← fossil
[2] assistant [CONTEXT COMPACTION ...] 14083 chars       ← OLD summary (previous round)
[3] user      [CONTEXT COMPACTION ...] 17576 chars       ← NEW summary
[4] ... live tail
```

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a long-lived session past the compression threshold; let it compact once.
2. Restart the gateway.
3. Let the session grow past the threshold again; the next compaction runs.
4. Inspect the API request: the previous summary and its protected neighbours sit verbatim above the new summary instead of being folded into it. Each further restart+compaction cycle stacks one more layer.

### Expected Behavior

For a previously-compacted session the protection stays decayed regardless of process restarts: the old summary is folded into the new one via the iterative-summary path, and the head stays `[system, new summary, tail]`.

### Actual Behavior

The compressor treats the post-restart compaction as the first one, re-protects `protect_first_n` head messages verbatim (old summary included), and appends the new summary after them. No error is logged — the transcript just silently accumulates dead summaries.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

### Debug Report

Not attached — this is a long-lived production instance with private conversation data. The sanitized dump excerpt above is from a full request dump; happy to share more targeted excerpts on request.

### Root Cause Analysis

`ContextCompressor._effective_protect_first_n` (`agent/context_compressor.py:2269` on current main, a6b9597):

```python
if self.compression_count >= 1 or self._previous_summary:
    return 0
return self.protect_first_n
```

Both decay guards — `compression_count` and `_previous_summary` — are **in-memory instance state**. A gateway restart recreates the compressor with `compression_count == 0` and `_previous_summary is None`, so the next compaction of an already-compacted session believes it is the first one and re-protects `protect_first_n` head messages verbatim.

The in-compress rehydration does not save it: `compress()` does rehydrate `_previous_summary` from the transcript (`_find_latest_context_summary`, `:2771`), but that scan runs **after** the head boundary is already fixed at `compress_start = self._protect_head_size(messages)` (`:2738`). So the rehydration only helps the *second* compaction within one process uptime. On a deployment with regular restarts, effectively every compaction is "first since restart" and the decay never fires at all.

The message roles in our dump corroborate the mechanism: round N head ended with a user message → summary inserted as `assistant` (alternation-driven role pick); after the restart, round N+1 protected `[user, assistant-summary]`, head now ends with `assistant` → new summary inserted as `user`. Both match the dump byte-for-byte.

### Proposed Fix

Three options, roughly in increasing order of robustness:

1. **Persist the decay state** — store a `was_compacted` boolean (or `compression_count`) in the session row and rehydrate it on session restore. Prevents new fossils, but leaves already-existing ones immortal.
2. **Derive instead of remember** (stateless, our preference) — decay to 0 whenever the current head already contains summary content. `_is_context_summary_content()` (`:2084`) already recognizes every summary prefix generation, and a head that contains a summary *is* a previously-compacted session. No stored counter, restart-proof by construction.
3. **Self-heal existing fossils** (independent hardening) — when assembling the compressed list, fold summary-content messages found in the protected head into the new summary window instead of re-protecting them. This kills fossils that already exist on the next pass; options 1–2 only prevent new ones.

Option 2 + 3 together both prevent and self-heal.

We can validate a fix under production traffic (long-lived Telegram sessions, frequent restarts during active development — which is how this surfaced).

### Related

- #11996 / #50001 — introduced the protect-decay this bug defeats.
- #12606 — per-turn rehydration on boot would incidentally fix the common case.
- #54923 — same family: compressor state that silently resets on restart.

items.title: feat(config): respect database.journal_mode from config.yaml — allow users to opt into DELETE mode on macOS/Linux

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Problem

`config.yaml` documents a `database:` section with `journal_mode`, `wal_autocheckpoint`, and `journal_size_limit` settings, but **none of these are ever read** by `SessionDB.__init__()` (#21807). The journal mode is hardcoded to WAL via `apply_wal_with_fallback()` on non-Windows platforms.

This forces macOS/Linux users who experience WAL-related data loss into patching `hermes_state.py` locally — a change that is overwritten on every `hermes update`.

## Real-world impact

We hit the exact scenario described in #30636: launchd sent SIGTERM to the gateway under high load, WAL pages were not checkpointed, and **an entire afternoon of conversation data was lost**. The root cause chain:

```
SIGTERM → WAL not checkpointed → uncommitted WAL pages lost → session data gone
```

Our workaround: patch `apply_wal_with_fallback()` to force `journal_mode=DELETE` instead of WAL. This eliminates the class of failure entirely — DELETE mode auto-rolls back the journal on next open, making the DB self-consistent after any crash.

However, this patch is a local modification that `hermes update` overwrites (git stash → pull → stash apply with potential conflicts → reset --hard). We have to maintain a post-merge hook to re-apply it after every update.

## Current official approach

| Platform | Journal mode | Rationale |
|----------|-------------|-----------|
| Windows | DELETE (forced) | #47007 — NTFS + WAL desyncs on abnormal shutdown |
| macOS | WAL + `checkpoint_fullfsync=1` | #54045 — makes checkpoints durable via F_FULLFSYNC |
| Linux | WAL | Default |

The `checkpoint_fullfsync=1` fix (#54045) reduces but does **not eliminate** the risk: it only guarantees durability at checkpoint boundaries. If SIGTERM arrives between checkpoints, in-flight WAL pages can still be lost. DELETE mode is the only mode that guarantees crash recovery without data loss, because SQLite auto-rolls back the journal on next open.

## Proposed solution

**Respect `database.journal_mode` from `config.yaml`** when set, with the following precedence:

1. **Windows**: always DELETE (current behavior from #47007, non-overridable)
2. **User config**: if `database.journal_mode` is explicitly set in config.yaml, use that value
3. **Default**: WAL on non-Windows (current behavior, unchanged)

This is a minimal, backward-compatible change:

```yaml
# config.yaml
database:
  journal_mode: DELETE    # opt-in: force DELETE on macOS/Linux
  wal_autocheckpoint: 200
  journal_size_limit: 10485760
```

When `journal_mode: DELETE` is set, `apply_wal_with_fallback()` should:
1. Checkpoint any existing WAL first (preserve pending data)
2. Switch to DELETE mode
3. Clean up orphaned `.db-wal` / `.db-shm` files (as #47007 does for Windows)

## Why not just use WAL + fullfsync?

For single-user deployments (the vast majority of Hermes installations), WAL provides no meaningful benefit over DELETE — there are no concurrent readers to take advantage of WAL's read-uncommitted isolation. The performance difference is negligible for interactive use (confirmed in #47007's testing).

WAL's advantage (concurrent reads during writes) only matters for multi-process setups (e.g., gateway + dashboard + TUI all reading state.db simultaneously). Users in that scenario can keep WAL; users who prioritize crash safety can opt into DELETE.

## Related

- #21807 — database PRAGMAs from config.yaml are never applied
- #30636 — state.db corruption from SIGTERM during launchd shutdown (macOS)
- #47007 — Force DELETE on Windows
- #54045 — F_FULLFSYNC barrier at WAL checkpoints on macOS
- #44503 — kanban.db already uses DELETE mode
- #32687 — No crash recovery path for corrupted state.db

items.title: [Bug]: Lazy backend refresh failures can corrupt venv, and update has no self-healing recovery

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Summary

When a lazy backend refresh fails during `hermes update` (e.g. `platform.matrix`), the failed `uv pip install` can leave empty package directories in the venv. Subsequent `hermes update` pulls new code that imports these now-broken packages, causing a crash loop with no recovery path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a lazy backend (e.g. `platform.matrix`) whose `uv pip install` fails — in our case due to pip 24.0 + setuptools build incompatibility when building `mautrix[encryption]` from source
2. `hermes update` runs `_refresh_active_lazy_features()` — the refresh fails with:
   ```
   ⚠ platform.matrix failed to refresh: pip install failed
   ```
3. The failed pip install leaves empty package directories (only `__pycache__` remains, `.py` files gone)
4. Next `hermes update` pulls new code that imports one of these broken packages → immediate crash:
   ```
   AttributeError: module 'yaml' has no attribute 'SafeDumper'
   ```
5. Update retries, same crash. **No way to recover** except manually reinstalling packages.

## Impact

- Hermes CLI completely broken
- `venv` must be repaired manually via `pip install --force-reinstall` for each corrupted package
- Affected packages in our case: yaml, dotenv, click, certifi, rich, cryptography, PyJWT, among others
- Happened repeatedly across 7 update runs in a short period

## Root Cause Analysis

1. **`_refresh_active_lazy_features()`** (hermes_cli/main.py:7557) catches exceptions but does not verify venv integrity after a failed install
2. pip 24.0 has known issues with setuptools build backends — upgrading to pip 26.1.2 resolved the build failure
3. The update flow runs new code immediately after `git pull` but has no fallback when imports fail

## Suggested Fix

**Short term:** Upgrade pip to a recent version in the update/bootstrap step — pip 24.0 (shipped with Python 3.11.15) has setuptools compatibility issues.

**Medium term:** In `_refresh_active_lazy_features()`, after a failure, run a lightweight venv integrity check (e.g. verify that a key packages `.py` files exist). If corruption is detected, offer to `pip install --force-reinstall` the broken package.

**Longer term:** The update flow should have a recovery path: if the new version fails to import, fall back to the previous venv state or attempt `pip install -e .[all]` before giving up.

items.title: [Bug]: Headless MCP OAuth blocks gateway startup with stale cached tokens

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

items.body:
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Bug description

A non-interactive `hermes gateway run` can remain in MCP OAuth discovery for the full browser-callback timeout before messaging adapters start. This still occurs when an OAuth token file exists but refresh/authorization falls back to a browser flow. After the first callback timeout, retries reuse the callback port and fail with `Address already in use`.

This was reproduced on a real Ubuntu 24.04 systemd user service running Hermes v0.16.0 / release 2026.6.5 at `3c231eb3979ab9c57d5cd6d02f1d577a3b718b43`. I also checked current `main` at `a6b9597d5fb92969d605a858d5f14536e805553a`: gateway discovery is still awaited before `runner.start()`, and the non-interactive OAuth guard still uses token-file existence rather than failing at the point where an interactive redirect/callback becomes necessary.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an enabled OAuth MCP server:

   ```yaml
   mcp_servers:
     example:
       enabled: true
       auth: oauth
       url: https://example.invalid/mcp
   ```

2. Ensure its token/client/metadata files exist, but arrange for the token refresh to fail such that the SDK begins authorization-code flow (expired/revoked token or stale client registration).
3. Start `hermes gateway run` from a systemd service or another process with non-TTY stdin.
4. Observe an authorization URL and localhost callback listener even though no operator can complete the flow.
5. Wait for the callback timeout. Subsequent connection retries attempt to bind the same port and may fail immediately with `OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use`.

Minimal red-capable seam: force non-interactive stdin, set a callback port, call `_wait_for_callback()`, and track `HTTPServer` construction. It currently attempts to bind a listener instead of rejecting the interactive flow before the bind.

## Expected behavior

- An optional MCP server must not delay gateway adapter startup or TUI readiness beyond a small configurable bound.
- Background/non-interactive discovery must never launch browser authorization or bind a callback listener. It should skip that MCP server promptly and emit one actionable warning, for example: run `hermes mcp login <server>` interactively, then restart/reload; or disable the server.
- Valid cached credentials should continue to work non-interactively, including refresh that does not require user authorization.
- If refresh falls back to authorization-code flow, the non-interactive guard must fail at that boundary regardless of whether a token file exists.
- Interactive OAuth retries/concurrent flows must not share or immediately rebind an unsafe callback-port global.

## Actual behavior

One observed gateway sequence:

```text
04:29:02  MCP OAuth: authorization required
04:34:02  OAuthNonInteractiveError: OAuth callback timed out — no authorization code received
04:34:04  OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use
04:34:04  initial connection failed (attempt 2/3)
04:34:07  OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use
04:34:11  failed initial connection after 3 attempts
```

Messaging initialization occurred only after MCP discovery returned. The first wait was five minutes; the retries then collided with the callback listener/port lifecycle.

## Root cause analysis

There are three interacting gaps:

1. Gateway startup awaits `run_in_executor(None, discover_mcp_tools)` before calling `runner.start()`. Moving blocking work to an executor preserves the event loop, but awaiting it still gates adapter startup.
2. OAuth's non-interactive guard only rejects when there is no token file. A cached-but-expired/revoked token passes the guard; when the SDK later invokes the redirect/callback handlers, `_wait_for_callback()` does not re-check interactivity and waits for the full timeout.
3. Callback state still depends on module-level `_oauth_port`, and `_wait_for_callback()` creates a fresh `HTTPServer` per flow. This is already tracked by #5344 and #44590; the deployed same-process retry reproduced the latter.

Related: #16856 moved gateway discovery into an executor but did not make gateway readiness independent of it. #54703 covers headless no-token behavior; this report is the cached-but-unusable token path.

## Proposed fix

- Start optional gateway MCP discovery asynchronously and wait only for a short configurable startup budget. Let adapters become ready when the budget expires, and refresh/rebuild MCP tool snapshots when late discovery completes.
- Carry an explicit `allow_interactive_oauth` execution context into discovery. At the redirect/callback boundary, raise an actionable `OAuthNonInteractiveError` before printing an authorization URL or binding a listener when interaction is disallowed. Do not infer permission solely from token-file existence.
- Resolve #5344/#44590 with per-flow callback state/ports or a safely persistent reusable callback server; avoid the module global and unsafe immediate rebind.

## Regression coverage requested

- Non-interactive gateway reaches adapter startup within the configured MCP discovery bound when OAuth needs browser authorization.
- TUI emits `gateway.ready` within the same bound and never consumes stdin for background OAuth.
- Cached valid/refreshable OAuth continues to connect non-interactively.
- Cached unusable OAuth skips promptly with an actionable warning and no callback bind.
- Repeated and concurrent interactive flows do not collide on callback ports.

## Environment

- Ubuntu 24.04
- Python 3.11.15
- Hermes v0.16.0 / 2026.6.5
- systemd user gateway service
- Also source-reviewed current main `a6b9597d5fb92969d605a858d5f14536e805553a`

No public `hermes debug share` link is included because the deployment logs/config contain private messaging and OAuth identifiers; the relevant sanitized sequence is above.
